title_en: The Breath That Poisoned the World
description_ru: Около 2,4 миллиарда лет назад микробы-фотосинтетики наполнили атмосферу кислородом и почти уничтожили собственную биосферу. История Великого кислородного события.
text:
Of all the catastrophes in the history of life, the most consequential was caused by a polluter so small that a billion of them would fit in a thimble, and so successful that its waste product now fills a fifth of the air we breathe. It is a tale that flatters no one, least of all the creature that tells it. We are accustomed to regarding oxygen as the very essence of vitality, and yet, for much of Earth's history, it was a toxin, and the microbes that first manufactured it in quantity were, from the standpoint of their neighbours, uncouth industrialists releasing fumes into a perfectly pleasant swamp.

For the first two billion years or so, the atmosphere contained virtually no free oxygen. The air, according to the best reconstructions, was composed mostly of nitrogen and carbon dioxide, with a fair amount of methane, and the oceans were rich in dissolved iron, which gave them a greenish cast. Life existed, but it was microbial, and its metabolism ran on sulphur, hydrogen, iron, and other chemical fuels. These organisms, the anaerobes, lived without oxygen, and for many of them, it would have been lethal.

The innovators probably arrived by about 2.7 billion years ago, and perhaps earlier. These were cyanobacteria, or at least their ancestors, and they had accomplished something miraculous: oxygenic photosynthesis, which uses sunlight to split water, taking the hydrogen and releasing the oxygen as a discard. Earlier forms of photosynthesis had used less abundant substances, such as hydrogen sulphide, and so were constrained by supply. Water, however, is everywhere. The cyanobacteria had discovered an inexhaustible raw material, and their numbers soared. Their fossil traces survive as layered mounds called stromatolites, and some still grow today in the warm shallows of Shark Bay in Western Australia, looking like a collection of badly made loaves.

For a long time, little seemed to happen, and the reason is a matter of simple chemistry. The first oxygen released into the oceans was immediately seized by the dissolved iron, which rusted out of the water and settled to the sea floor as fine layers of iron oxide. These deposits, banded with alternating stripes of rust-red and grey, are known as banded iron formations, and they are the source of most of the iron ore that now builds our cities and our cars. In a sense, the planet had a vast sponge, and the oxygen had to saturate it before any could escape. The same process occurred with volcanic gases and with minerals on land.

There were, it seems, false dawns. Chemical clues in rocks a few hundred million years older than the main event hint at brief and local "whiffs" of oxygen, perhaps in sheltered pools of water above the cyanobacterial mats, which then faded as quickly as breath on a window. The picture is still being drawn, and its edges are blurred by the simple fact that rocks billions of years old are seldom well preserved. Geologists, who are a patient tribe, have learnt to reason from a handful of grains of sulphur and a few smears of rust.

Eventually, between about 2.4 and 2.2 billion years ago, the sponge was full. Oxygen began to accumulate in the atmosphere, in what geologists call the Great Oxidation Event. The evidence is subtle but compelling. Sulphur in ancient rocks older than that date carries a peculiar isotopic signature, produced by ultraviolet light reacting with gases in an oxygen-free atmosphere; after the event, the signature vanishes. Fossil soils, too, show that iron minerals were no longer washed away but stayed behind, rusting in place, and the first red beds, sandstones tinted by oxidised iron, appear in the geological record.

It would be pleasant to report that the world rejoiced. Instead, it suffered a grave crisis. Oxygen is a highly reactive element; it will tear at fragile molecules and, in the cells of organisms unprepared for it, it produces damaging by-products. Many anaerobic microbes were driven into the muddy refuges where oxygen could not follow, and a great number of lineages presumably vanished. Because microbes leave scant fossils, we cannot count the dead, but the evidence of chemical changes suggests an upheaval on a planetary scale.

The atmosphere, moreover, was affected in another way. Methane is a far more potent greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide, and it had probably helped to keep the young Earth warm, since the Sun was then roughly a sixth fainter than it is today. Oxygen destroyed methane, converting it to carbon dioxide and water. The warming blanket was thinned, and the planet may have plunged into a sequence of glaciations, known as the Huronian glaciation, whose deposits are found in what is now Canada. Some researchers consider that ice may have reached the tropics, though the details remain contested. The polluters, in other words, had cooled their own planet.

And yet, as so often in the history of life, a disaster proved an opportunity. Some lineages did not merely tolerate oxygen but learned to exploit it. Respiration with oxygen releases far more energy from a given amount of food than any anaerobic alternative, and the cells that harnessed it gained an enormous advantage. Around that time, or somewhat later, one such cell engulfed a bacterium that was adept at the trick, and the descendant of that bacterium, the mitochondrion, now powers every complex animal, plant and fungus. Our ancestors, in short, were refugees who found the toxic air profitable.

Later still, oxygen would climb to the levels required for large animals, and a layer of ozone would form in the upper atmosphere, shielding the land from ultraviolet radiation and allowing life to leave the water. But the pivotal act had occurred long before, in a world of shallow seas and tiny green cells, when something unimaginably small altered the composition of an entire planet. It is a humbling reflection that every breath we take is, in a sense, the aftermath of an ancient environmental disaster, and that we exist because a handful of microbes, with no malice and no foresight, polluted the world.

questions.question: Which organisms first produced oxygen in quantity?
What happened to the first oxygen released into the oceans?
questions.answer: It reacted with dissolved iron, forming banded iron formations.

questions.question: Why was the Great Oxidation Event a crisis?
questions.answer: Oxygen was toxic to anaerobes and destroyed methane, cooling the planet.

questions.question: What benefit did oxygen eventually bring?
questions.answer: More energy from respiration, leading to mitochondria and complex life.
